Dear City Council,
    My name is Micheal Medeiros, and I am a long time resident of this great city. I'm writing today in regard to councils proposal to convert our beautiful green space located in Greenfield Park into an urban livestock pen. It is my opinion that such an act would have a large negative impact on our city, and it's citizens.  
    As you may know, current green space within the city is very limited as it is. This valuable space serves as a place for citizens to escape the confines of the city and enjoy the fresh air provided by mother nature. Transforming this precious resource into livestock pens will quickly consume this valuable resource and transform it into a barren wasteland. The reason such practice is normally reserved to rural areas is because livestock need to be rotated through segregated fields in order for vegetation to be allowed to regrow. Introducing livestock into such a limited space will make this practice impossible.

 

    While it is hopeful that our current drought will end, it's a fact of the present that drought conditions have made water a scarce commodity. Livestock require vast amounts of water to thrive. City water is expensive to produce due to the fact that humans require a quality of water unparalleled by livestock. Considering current conditions, it would be expensive to provide such a precious resource to livestock. Rural areas surrounding the city would be much more suited for such an endeavour due to their ability to provide natural water sources suitable to livestock, at much cheaper rates. 

    Regardless of the current cost of food, raising livestock in an urban setting comes with too many costs to tip the scales. Besides the high cost of water, their waste will have to be disposed of. On rural farms, this is accomplished easily by using this byproduct as fertilizer on neighbouring fields. In an urban setting, this cost will be born by our waste management system, and instead of being recycled, the costs to dispose of this waste will inevitably be passed on to the citizens of the city. This waste product also brings with it other costs that are difficult to quantify.

    

    Animal waste is inherently toxic. Not only will the smell be incredibly displeasing to the surrounding residents, but the diseases that such waste can transmit is an unnecessary hazard to create within a densely populated area. While the city maintains that leases can be terminated if cleanliness and animal welfare aren't meeting the standards, this hazard will be impossible to avoid as maintaining perfect cleanliness at all times is simply impossible. 
    

    While an urban livestock initiative seems pleasing in thought, we must also consider the purpose of this livestock is as a food source. This requires that such livestock eventually be put to death and butchered. This practice is one that is best left away from residential areas and outside the city where things can be done in private.

    While I agree that livestock is an integral part of our way of life, and is an immensely valuable resource to humanity, it's my opinion that this is not the time or place for such an endeavour. When we consider the drought, the health risks, and the costs, it's hard to argue that an urban setting is a suitable setting to raise livestock. I strongly urge council to reconsider this proposal and instead consider finding an area away from such a densely populated residential area, with ample space and natural water sources. 

    Thank you,

 Micheal Medeiros

Regards,

John Doe

To whom it may concern,

I've recently been notified that management is considering a series of rules that, in effect, constitute a ban on personal cellphones here at Company Co. Ltd. I believe there are several reasons as to why such a policy could be considered both an ethical breach of personal autonomy and a significant safety issue.

We're told that a younger demographic spends an average of slightly over sixty minutes on their phone during work hours, and given a generalized overview of the kind of apps they tend towards using during that time. I believe that the purpose of this information is to negatively characterize the people using their cellphones; organizing the people using their phones into arbitrary age groups allows some of the groups to villainize others as being the source of the problem, despite the likelihood that outliers at all ages have skewed this data one way or another. There's also the implication that the usage is largely for frivolous purposes, with social media and games making up a significant percentage of the total time. I believe that what is being done in non-productive time is not really relevant to whether it is non-productive, and as such the focus on it is unwarranted.

 

My experiences have taught me that distraction is a symptom of disengagement - it's generally fruitless to try and minimize distraction to maintain productivity. A distracted person may be going through various personal crises, such as ongoing health issues, problems with relationships, financial difficulties, etc. This can negatively impact their capacity for engagement in all areas of their lives, work included, and the need for mild disengagement serves as an unconscious coping mechanism. It may also be the case that disengagement can be caused by the person's relationship with their job - if a person is stressed by a lack of proper training, or feeling underappreciated, or undue competition in the workplace, this can manifest as a disinterest in productivity. Rather than spend time and effort trying to police whatever people's disengagements manifest as, whether it be a scroll through social media or the folding of a paper airplane, I believe it would be more productive to direct those resources into creating and maintaining systems that allow management to engage with employees to determine how to fulfill their needs and encourage them, so that they may feel properly engaged by their position.

 

Management also suggests that safety is an issue, presenting an anecdote wherein an employee at Paragon Building Supplies accidentally drove a forklift into a co-worker. While workplace safety should be a paramount concern to any legitimate place of business, I believe that companies engaged in areas such as construction and building tend to engage with dangerous machinery more often than we do here, and as such their safety concerns are of a magnitude higher than ours. As you are aware, Company Co Ltd.'s main area of production is artisanal, handcrafted clown wigs, and other than the tragic, catastrophic events of July 19th, 2017, we simply do not have equipment that would necessitate such a degree of oversight of personal actions. 

 

Even if we were to evaluate the situation based on the forklift collision incident, I believe it behooves us to consider that phones are just that - a phone, primarily a means of communication. A worker driving a forklift went to answer his phone when it rang, causing an incident - I think that the prudent thing to do would have been to simply stop the forklift before answering the phone. It should go without saying that any machinery should be operated at full attention, and that if you find your attention veering off to some other distraction, this is not the distraction's fault. Also, I believe that it's important to ask, what was the call? While it's easy to mentally characterize the forklift operator as easily distracted, it could be the case that the call was from or about someone important. What if the operator has a specific ringtone for a call from his spouse, and he knows his spouse wouldn't be calling unless it were an emergency? Details like this are important when talking about an isolated event, as they allow us to be aware of the granularity of situations that occur and not make overly harsh judgments about the people involved or their actions.

 

Having mentioned that phones are primarily tools for communication and the situations in which the capacity for communication is important, I believe that it is evident that the safety benefits of access to a personal cellphone outweigh the few consequences. What do I do if I need to pick up my daughter from clown college for emergency reasons, and she can't get in contact with me? What would Clancy Higgins have done on that fateful July evening, when he was slowly being smothered to death by tens of thousands of toppled clown wigs, if he didn't have access to his phone with which to contact the fire department to rescue him? What if that one firefighter didn't have her phone on her, to contact further rescue services once the fire department, too, was consumed by the mass of wigs? We may have lost many more lives that day, and I shudder to think of it.

 

While I understand management's concerns about productivity and safety, I believe that the sacrifices we would thereby be making to our autonomy and to our safety would not be worth the risk. I entered this industry to fulfill my fiery, passionate need to make the best clown wigs that money can buy, but if these are the kind of personal sacrifices I would be expected to make to live that dream, then I may find myself considering returning to my elephant-focused veterinary practice. I urge you to reconsider this proposal as soon as possible.

 

All the best,

Julian Bryant

You must also consider the effect on the community, because keeping animals involves unpleasant smells, sights and precautions. Then, there is also the effect on the city when it comes to the resources provided to owners and the livestock that they keep.

 

Animals, like humans, experience a stress response to overstimulation. There are many stimuli that they are especially sensitive to; such as sounds, sights, and feeling crowded. Sounds in the city are a whirlwind of sensory overload. There are honking cars, and frustrated pedestrians that may shout in response to a vehicle honking at them. Construction around the city using heavy machinery, jackhammers, and similar tools create a variety of screeching and banging. Then there is the visual aspect of an overstimulating environment. Street lights, and headlamps on vehicles are constantly changing and passing by. There are likely many people, possibly with dogs, on the surrounding sidewalks walking by the area. There may even be extra curiosity surrounding the plot and therefore more bystanders around the area watching the novelty of keeping animals within city limits. These things can lead to the feeling of being crowded in a small space in addition to being around a number of other animals, that limit I have not seen advertised yet. Animals need adequate space to combat the stressor of feeling trapped from crowding. Stress on animals leads to things like decline, failure to thrive and illness.

 

Consider the effect it will have on the community as well. Keeping animals is a messy process. Bodily functions are involved, including urine, bowel movements and the body's response to injury; which could include blood, pus, mucous and the like. Some residents have commented that they are not enthused at the idea of being near enough to experience these smells and sights while commuting or enjoying themselves out at a restaurant. There is also a rise in transferable illness and disease between animals and humans, according to a recent broadcast in the news. As I've previously stated, illness is often a response to stress. We should also ask if out kids are ready for the conversation about death. As there is a possibility of loss of life due to illness and stress on the animals. There is also the fact that many of these animals will be raised to be consumed by their owners. That is a lesson that children struggle to comprehend and cope with at a young age. Even if the owners' children are prepared, children that pass by may form an attachment to seeing an animal every day. The sudden disappearance of that animal will possibly be a difficult conversation and lesson the parents will have to teach, unprepared.

 

Finally, we should consider the effect this rezoning will have on the city. Water and building materials will be provided to the owners at no additional expense outside the lease rental. The city will also have to closely monitor the leaseholders' ability to care for their animals or else face termination of their lease. Animals improperly cared for will increase frustration from the community about smell and unpleasant sights of improper care of animals.

 

In conclusion, I am in disagreement about this proposal. The risk to the animals from improper care, stress, and illness is too great. The existence of the animals in a populated space will create conflicting interests in the community and make many frustrated with the unwanted smell and sight of animals. Our children in the city may not be ready for the uncomfortable realization of animals raised as a food source. In addition, the funding has potential to be a great expense and the city may face a water shortage that will be further made an issue by giving free water to the urban livestock area that will require a lot of water. I suggest that the city strongly considers all these points I've made.

 

Thank you for your time.

 

Molly Johnson

December 5, 2024

 

Dear City Council,

I am in disagreement with the city's proposal to rezone one of our community green spaces to allow urban livestock for several reasons including odour, noise and human neglect.  This proposal should be taken very serious and researched extensively before a decision is made that may leave the taxpayer to foot the bill.  I grew up on a mixed farm with cattle, pigs and chickens and believe the problems that may arise will far outweigh the benefits.

 

An area dedicated to urban livestock will bring with it a level of smell and noise that can only be controlled to a certain extent.  The pens can be kept as clean as possible, but there will always be some level of smell that not all the surrounding businesses or homes will appreciate.  It is natural for animals to make noise and that cannot be controlled especially during the night.  A lot of different animal species put together in a controlled area may cause them to make even more noise than a regular rural setting.

 

I think a lot of people would be very excited about this idea until they actually realized the cost and time that would have to go into such a commitment.  There is a yearly lease fee, purchasing the animals, and feeding them.  Sure, you get free water and housing materials, but the cost to feed such animals is not cheap.  The time commitment to take care of these animals is extensive as well.

 

I also disagree with this proposal as people may lose interest in a short period of time just as they do with the latest fad or trend.  What will happen to those animals if that were to be the case?  The person could complete their lease application and the Livestock Education Program, but then six months down the road when they realize how much work and cost have to go into it, they are no longer interested.  If that should happen then someone from the city will have to step in to take over these duties and costs to make sure the animals are not being neglected.  That in turn will affect the taxpayers.

 

At the end of the day, buying eggs and meat from the store could be the more viable option.  I suppose there could be some learning experiences and fun along the way for our children and perhaps the adults, but in the long run it is not a practical idea.  I know my years of growing up on the farm included seven days a week of hard work and commitment.  It is a lot of time, energy and money to look after animals and I don't think that belongs in the middle of an urban setting.

Dear Council,

 

    As a proud resident of this community, I would like to voice my personal opinion in rejection of the recent proposal for rezoning communal green spaces. 

    While I must acknowledge the potential to offset the cost of living increases we are all experiencing, I disagree with the proposition that the best course of action to avert this growing crisis is through local livestock husbandry. Livestock, as with most forms of food production, is undeniably most profitable and efficient when it can benefit from economies of scale. To claim that small-scale hobby farming would have any significant benefit to the community's average cost of food is absurd. Given the small size of the community, I would argue that it is in the average resident's best interest for funds to be allocated to subsidize industrially produced staples like grains and dairy. 

    It is impossible to have a discussion on farming and animal husbandry without mentioning its consumption of our most basic finite resources, land and water. While livestock offer some advantages over farming, the former's inherent resource requirements does not lend itself to developed urban areas. Crops require nutrient rich, well draining soil and extensive irrigation. However, it can be grown at much higher densities than livestock, while using less water to produce similar caloric density. Livestock benefits from not needing nutrient dense soil, only rich enough to support simple grasses and shrubbery. Instead, livestock require exorbitant amounts of water as compared with modern, irrigated crop fields. It is therefore typically raised in large rural areas with low water requirements, that cannot support more profitable cash crops. Given our regional increase in water usage and projected droughts in 7 out of 10 cities, it would not make sense to proliferate an industry known for its extensive consumption of this precious resource.

    It is wholly inadvisable to go forward with this proposition and rezone our valuable green spaces and replace them with what is little more than a token amount of livestock. The costs far outweigh any potential benefits. Any problem it attempts to address can be handled more efficiently through other means that will not deplete our finite resources.

 

Sincerely,

Local Resident

    The 5.0 City Proposal for Urban Livestock has been a source of conjecture and debate among city residents ever since it was first brought to the table. While some members of the community may vouch for the easy of access to affordable food the proposal is purported to bring with it, other members of the community including myself find such an idea worrying. Animal-related and animal-spread diseases and illnesses are not only on the rise right now, but there are many cases in history of livestock and urban wildlife aiding in the spread of disease and illness. Black Death, Mad Cow Disease, H1Z1, and Avian Flu are all just a handful of examples of the diseases that spring to mind when the question of urban livestock comes up. 

 

    It is also worth considering the predictions that the vast majority of cities in our country will be facing water shortages this summer. With weather and climate change getting evermore unpredictable and harsh, is the money required to keep all these animals healthy and happy in the middle of these weather conditions really something the average citizen of our city wants to deal with? Should Jebediah Clancy, 87-year-old owner of Clancy's Bookstore, have to pay more taxes just so his city can fund a livestock plot he doesn't partake in? Do we want to be rationing the water we will already be short on to livestock that could easily be replaced by food banks? Will the community still be happy with the livestock plot when we're not simply sharing, but RATIONING our essential, life-giving resources with them?

 

    I propose an alternative be considered: the land currently proposed for the location of the livestock be used for homeless shelter, food bank, and a community garden. For those members of the community interested in sourcing their own food to save money, they would retain the option of a community area for food. The homeless have shelter during extreme weather, and people who do not have the time to put into livestock or the garden could simply attend the food bank.

I doubt the owners and proprietors of businesses and homes in the area would appreciate the sudden rise in stench and noise from the animals. It's also worth considering that regardless of safety measures, animals will eventually escape the enclosures no matter what reasonable steps are taken to prevent it, presumably without making the entire plot look like a small animal prison which would inevitably bring down citizen morale across the city.

The idea itself isn't an inherently bad idea. An urban livestock plot does serve purpose. But this is not the time for it, especially with the question of whether the city could appropriately supply the livestock with water in this coming summer or not still up in the air.

 

    The city has shown a great concern for the environment and their citizens with the introduction of the 5.0 City Proposal. However, we simply find ourselves in an inappropriate time for such an idea and there are better, more attractive, longer-lived solutions for the problems the livestock plot would address. I hope the city considers this. Thank you for reading.

Dear City council,

    I'm writing in response to the request for feedback on the proposal to rezone a community green space. I've surveyed residents and businesses in the neighbourhood and have gathered information and opinions from a variety of sources, which I'm happy to present to you now. I'm not necessarily the best writer, but I'll do my best, and I thank you for this opportunity.

    I want to make it clear from the start that everyone I've spoken with disagrees with the proposal, and that is also my personal view. I will use this letter to explain our perspective, with the hope that our input will be considered in the final decision.

    Food insecurity and the environment are big issues and have been hammered home by the side promoting this proposal. Of course, we all want to do our part to promote and consume local products, but we aren't convinced raising livestock in an urban area is the solution. "Consuming local" doesn't have to mean "literally from outside your doorstep", and there are many ways to promote the environment.

    In fact, it seems to us that the environment could also be served by having more shrubs and trees in the proposed area -- perhaps even a botanical garden that would encourage our neighbourhood's residents and visitors to get out and breathe clean, fresh air. In particular, the elderly residents currently have a lack of exercise and socializing opportunities in our neighbourhood, and none of them relish the thought of going for a walk in an urban farm.

    The proposal isn't for farmers to run a farm in our green space, but for residents to do so. None of the residents I've spoken to are interested in this proposal, so I have to assume that the "residents" will be people from other neighbourhoods who'll use our green space to fulfill their rural fantasies. We feel that many of these people will treat their "farms" in our neighbourhood as hobbies and not always be on hand to take care of their animals. This is especially relevant considering the application fee is so cheap. What's going to happen when it snows, or when the animals are sick, or when the "farmer" wants to go on holiday? A real farmer has knowledge and networks -- and passion! These hobby farmers will probably tire of the whole exercise, and it will fall to residents to try to pick up the pieces. The city claims tenants will have to be "educated" and that it will be able to terminate leases, but we're not confident that will be done in a timely way -- and, even if the leases are terminated, what will happen to the animals then? It's a recipe for total mayhem!

    Proponents have focused on rabbits as cute, furry mascots of this proposal. It's harder to argue against these cuddly creatures, but in fact, the proposal allows for all kinds of other animals to be moved to our green space -- including the noisier and smellier varieties! This is ridiculous, and borderline dishonest! If rabbits are the intended goal, then there should be restrictions on the random sheep, ducks, goats, and chickens. (The graphic also includes turkeys, but it's not clear if those are also a part of the proposal?!)

    To be honest, we feel that we have been dismissed and unfairly portrayed in some councillors' statements to local media as NIMBYs. This makes us feel disrespected and looked-down-on by City elites, as if our views were less important than the fantasies of the folks from other neighbourhoods who want to use our green spaces. But it's not that we're blindly opposed to everything. We want to boost entrepreneurial skills and enable our children to learn about animals and the farm-to-table movement, and that is why we would like to present an alternative proposal.

    As the attached map makes clear, our neighbourhood is currently set on city limits, and there's plenty of unoccupied green space just a few hundred metres from the proposed location of this urban farm, which could be used instead. Apparently, this option was never considered (we wonder why!), but we feel it could be a viable alternative, and also prove that we're willing to host initiatives such as this urban farm "in our backyard". 

    In conclusion, we feel we've made several reasoned arguments against the current proposal. Inexplicably, these failed to be considered at the earlier planning stages, and we hope it's not already too late to bring them up. At the very least, the application fee should be significantly raised, and the type of animals allowed should be restricted to rabbits. But we feel that our proposal to move the proposed location is the best and most likely to benefit the neighbourhood, and the City. Perhaps, funds could then be allocated to transform this green space into a genuine green hub that could boost community spirit and the attractiveness of our neighbourhood. We would welcome any future consideration of such investment plans.

 

Thank you again for your time. We look forward to your response.

The Concerned Neighbourhood Residents.

Good morning Chief Smith,

 

I am contacting you with regard to the recent proposed changes to the workplace Policy and Procedures that reflects on the use of personal cell phones within the Firehall.  I endorse the changes proposed by the committee and agree that personal cell phones should not be used during operational time while on duty, and only on personal time during the shift.

 

As a veteran member of the fire crew, I am experienced in our 24-hour shifts.   There are many opinions on the use of personal cell phones within our work environment, but I sincerely believe that there are some strong points on the proposed policy.

 

As you are aware, our operational time in which we are required for firefighting duties are 07:00 to 12:00 then 13:00 to 14:30, followed by duties between 18:00 to 20:00 hours.  The variable to these times are when on an emergency or service call, as required by our Community.

 

Our shift normally begins with vehicle testing and inventory.  This means set up of the 105' aerial, as well as pump cycling and using heavy hydraulics to test the jaws of life.  Recently, there was a workplace injury at Paragon Building Supplies in Belleville, where a forklift operator accidently veered a forklift he was operating, into a co-worker when he was distracted by his cell phone ringing.  We also had Firefighter Foster get injured last year while using his cell phone and not noticing his ring trapped in the ladder as he came down from the top of the pumper, while he held his cell phone.  This resulted in his finger skin being partially gloved.

 

This is all about safety in the work environment.  Focus is required when using heavy equipment.  By removing the option of personal cell phones during operational time, we are being proactive under the guidelines and intentions of Occupational Health and Safety.

 

By limiting access to personal cell phones during specific times, we most likely increase productivity in our workplace.  When we have tours of the firehall, the public, and specifically the children want to be engaged with our firefighters on a personal level and learn about our careers.  I believe it is a bad example for a firefighter to be using his personal cell phone rather than promoting fire safety in our Community. Last year we had the issue of the bolts on the rear tires of the pumper backing off which caused damage to the rim and had the potential of causing injury to others.  This could have been prevented with a thorough maintenance inspection by our members.  Minor distractions can lead to dangerous results, and have a tendency to spiral and morph into an "accident."

 

I am also of the thought that our training evolutions will be more beneficial to our members without the interference of personal cell phones.  Be it hands-on physical training or computer based training, it has been proven in Adult Education practices that uninterrupted training allows for an increased retention for the student.

Be it Facebook or TikTok or other platforms, we have seen firefighters terminated by their Municipality for negative Social Media posts. Rather than a circle of people looking at their cell phones, we can more fully interact, communicate and become a stronger team.  We are not just a team, we are a family.  I look forward to becoming a stronger and safer link to this, within the Belleville Fire Department.

 

Thank you for your consideration.  In Fire Safety,

 

 

 

 

Carson I. Cross,

Training Officer.
